You then have a 15-day window with reminders to reply by tapping in the app, clicking the email button, or replying on WhatsApp. Only an explicit reply resets the countdown; using the app does not. hub.title: How Keeplas protects your legacy.
hub.intro: Keeplas is a life-continuity platform. We combine a zero-knowledge vault, a multi-channel life check and a social recovery network so your digital legacy outlives you, on your terms.

hero.title: Your key never leaves your device.
hero.body: The master key that unlocks your vault is generated and stored only on your devices. Keeplas servers hold encrypted blobs plus the public metadata needed to orchestrate life checks, nothing more. Even we cannot read your vault.

vault.title: Digital Vault
vault.description: Zero-knowledge storage for documents, credentials, financial assets and digital legacy. Everything is encrypted on your device before it leaves.

lifeCheck.title: Life Check
lifeCheck.description: Automated proof-of-life over WhatsApp and email. Verify each channel once so we can reach you (app push coming soon). Configurable cadence, a 15-day response window with reminders, and a travel-mode pause for trips.

letters.title: Letters & Messages
letters.description: Sealed letters released by specific life events or dates. Compose them as a Letter / Message item from your vault. Recipients receive them once curators validate the trigger.

emergency.title: Acute emergencies
emergency.description: For accidents and sudden illness, your phone's native Medical ID is on the lock screen, recognized by paramedics, and works offline. Here is how to set it up.

trustedContacts.title: Trusted Contacts
trustedContacts.description: At least two trust contacts hold encrypted shards of your master key. They confirm your unavailability and reconstruct the vault when needed. Recipients receive your pre-assigned content separately.

recovery.title: Recovery & Inheritance
recovery.description: Two paths: 24-word phrase for self-service recovery, Shamir social recovery via trust contacts when the phrase is lost or after you become unreachable. Default threshold: 2 trusted contacts.

insights.title: Reflect & Prepare
insights.description: Nine honest cases: reflective questions, real pain points, emergency essentials, and the cryptographic foundations behind Keeplas. ~10 minutes to read.

zeroKnowledge.title: Zero-knowledge encryption
zeroKnowledge.body: Your master key is derived locally and never sent to Keeplas. Every vault item is encrypted with AES-256-GCM before upload. Keeplas servers see only ciphertext.

shamir.title: Shamir secret sharing
shamir.body: Your master key is split into 4 cryptographic shards: one device shard and up to three trusted-contact shards. Recovery starts working from 2 trusted contacts with the default threshold. Reconstruction always happens on your contacts' devices, never on Keeplas servers.

auditLog.title: Hash-chained audit log
auditLog.body: Every action writes an immutable tamper-evident entry. Each log hash links to the previous one; rewriting history would break the chain.

recoveryKit.title: Recovery kit on paper
recoveryKit.body: Export a printable document with your 24-word phrase. Cold-storage only. Keeplas does not store the phrase nor any hash of it. The phrase derives your Root Key locally via Argon2id.

lifecycle.heading: What happens after inactivity
lifecycle.readMore: Read the full recovery & inheritance flow

cadence.title: A check-in opens
cadence.body: Your cadence passes without an explicit 'I'm well'. Keeplas opens a Life Check cycle and starts a 15-day response window. Using the app does not count. Only an explicit reply does.

window.title: Every channel reaches you
window.body: WhatsApp and email fire together at day 0, with reminders at day 3, 7 and 10 (app push coming soon). One tap, the email button, or a WhatsApp reply resets the countdown.

confirmation.title: Trust contacts confirm unreachability
confirmation.body: No reply across the whole window. Your trust contacts are asked to confirm they can't reach you, within the window you set (default 7 days) and to the number you require. Nothing is released yet.

grace.title: Last chance to come back
grace.body: Once enough contacts confirm, a fixed 72-hour grace window opens, separate from the confirmation window. Sign in and click I am well and the cycle is cancelled. Nothing leaves the vault.

release.title: Vault opens for inheritance
release.body: When the grace expires, contacts submit their shards. Threshold reached → master key reconstructed on their device → vault opens read-only → recipients receive their pre-assigned items.

quickLinks.heading: Jump to a feature
quickLinks.subtitle: All documentation is inline with the product: each screen has its own guided empty state and tooltips.

vault.title: Digital Vault
vault.intro: Zero-knowledge storage for documents, credentials, financial assets and your digital legacy. Everything is encrypted on your device before it ever leaves it. Keeplas only ever holds ciphertext.

onDevice.title: Encrypted on-device
onDevice.body: Each item is encrypted with AES-256-GCM in your browser before upload. Plaintext never travels over the network.

yourKey.title: Your key, your key
yourKey.body: The master key that unlocks your vault is derived locally from your 24-word phrase and never sent to Keeplas.

blind.title: Servers stay blind
blind.body: Keeplas stores only encrypted blobs plus the public metadata needed to orchestrate recovery. Even we cannot read your vault.

documents.title: Documents
documents.body: Identity papers, contracts, wills, insurance policies: any file that matters to your succession.

credentials.title: Credentials
credentials.body: Passwords, access codes and account details, sealed behind your master key.

financial.title: Financial assets
financial.body: Bank accounts, investments and crypto holdings, with the context your heirs need to act.

letters.title: Letters & Messages
letters.body: Time-released letters sealed until a date or life event. See the Letters & Messages guide.

storage.heading: Storage included
storage.body: The Free plan includes 100 MB of encrypted storage. The Lifetime plan raises it to 10 GB. Encryption overhead is counted against your quota.

lifeCheck.title: Life Check
lifeCheck.intro: A transparent proof-of-life system. Keeplas reaches you over WhatsApp and email on a cadence you set; an explicit reply resets the countdown. Only prolonged silence ever moves your vault toward recovery.

verifyChannel.title: Verify each channel once
verifyChannel.body: Confirm your WhatsApp number and email so we can reliably reach you. App push is coming soon.

cadence.title: Set your cadence
cadence.body: Choose how often a check-in opens. Between cycles, Keeplas stays silent.

window.title: A 15-day window with reminders
window.body: When a cycle opens, WhatsApp and email fire at day 0, with reminders at day 3, 7 and 10.

reply.title: An explicit reply resets it
reply.body: One tap in the email, or a WhatsApp reply, resets the countdown. Browsing the app does not count. Only an explicit 'I'm well'.

travel.title: Travel mode
travel.body: Pause checks for a trip so a missed message never escalates while you're away.

visible.title: Always visible
visible.body: A live countdown shows exactly where you stand. No hidden timers, no silent resets.

afterInactivity.heading: What happens if you don't respond
afterInactivity.body: If the whole 15-day window passes with no reply, your trust contacts are asked to confirm they can't reach you. Only then, after a further confirmation window and a 72-hour grace period, does recovery begin. You can cancel at any point by signing in and clicking I am well.
afterInactivity.readMore: Read the full recovery & inheritance flow

letters.title: Letters & Messages
letters.intro: Sealed letters released by a specific date or life event. You compose them as a vault item, encrypted like everything else, and recipients receive them only once your curators validate the trigger.

compose.title: Compose from your vault
compose.body: Create a Letter / Message item alongside your documents. It is encrypted on-device, like any other vault item.

recipients.title: Assign recipients
recipients.body: Pre-assign each letter to the people who should receive it. Recipients need no shard and no action of their own.

trigger.title: Set the trigger
trigger.body: Release on a fixed date, or on a life event such as your vault opening for inheritance.

validated.title: Released after validation
validated.body: Recipients receive the letter once your curators confirm the trigger has been met, never before.

privacy.heading: Sealed until the moment
privacy.body: A letter stays encrypted in your vault until its trigger fires. Keeplas servers only ever hold ciphertext, so no one (not us, not the recipient, not your curators) can read it ahead of time.

trustedContacts.title: Trusted Contacts
trustedContacts.intro: The people you designate to protect your vault, both during your life (in case you lose access) and after (for your digital succession). One unified role, one mental model.

trust.title: Trust contact
trust.body: Helps you recover access if you lose your phone, confirms you are unreachable, and receives the items you assigned to them once your vault is released. Never holds a key to your vault.

bullets.noCap: No cap: invite as many as you need
bullets.receives: Receives only the items you assign, after the vault unlocks
bullets.moments: Active role at three moments: invitation, escalation, recovery

accept.title: Accepts the invitation
accept.body: To invite them you provide their name, email, and optionally their phone number. They receive an email with a one-time link. When they accept and create their own vault, those identifiers are pre-filled and locked on the signup form, so their account matches the identity you registered. They sign in to Keeplas, which generates their own ML-KEM keypair on-device; the public key is uploaded so you can wrap their shard to it.

receive.title: Receives their shard (silently)
receive.body: When you click Distribute now, your client wraps their Shamir share to their public key and stores the ciphertext on the server. The next time they open /shared-with-me, their browser unwraps it on-device, persists the raw bytes in their IndexedDB, and stamps lastVerifiedAt as cryptographic proof that the unwrap worked. No manual click, no copy-paste, and Keeplas servers never see the raw shard.

confirm.title: Confirms unreachability (if needed)
confirm.body: If your Life Check escalates and you stop responding, all your trust contacts are notified. Each can mark you as unreachable from their hub. Once the threshold is reached, a 72-hour grace window opens, during which you can still cancel by signing in.

submit.title: Submits their shard at recovery
submit.body: After the grace window expires (or you manually trigger social recovery), contacts open /shared-with-me and click Submit my shard. Their browser pulls their shard from IndexedDB, wraps a copy for every peer's public key, and uploads the envelopes. The contact never sees, types, or exports the raw bytes. Once the threshold is reached, any submitter can click Reconstruct master key: their device fetches the wrapped-for-them envelopes, unwraps them, combines with its own raw shard, and rebuilds the master key entirely on-device. Servers see only ciphertext throughout.

threshold.heading: How many contacts must agree?
threshold.body: You choose the recovery threshold during onboarding. Threshold 2 is the default and works from 2 trusted contacts. Threshold 3 is stricter and requires 3 ready contacts.

emergencyInfo.title: Use your phone's built-in Medical ID.
emergencyInfo.intro: Keeplas focuses on long-term continuity: inheritance, life check, shard-based recovery. For accidents and sudden illness, the fastest and most reliable tool is already on your phone's lock screen, works offline, and is recognized by trained paramedics. Two minutes to set up.

why.heading: Why not a Keeplas card?
why.body: A QR card with your medical info would have to be readable without a key, meaning unencrypted on our servers. That contradicts our zero-knowledge promise. Apple and Google already solved this on the device itself: the data lives on your phone, accessible from the lock screen without unlocking, and never reaches a third-party server.

open.title: Open the Health app
open.body: Pre-installed on every iPhone (white icon, red heart). If you removed it, reinstall from the App Store.

profile.title: Tap your profile, then Medical ID
profile.body: Top-right corner of Health → your initials → Medical ID.

fill.title: Fill in the essentials
fill.body: Name, date of birth, blood type, allergies, medications, conditions, height, weight, organ donor status. Add at least one emergency contact (with the relationship: Mother, Spouse…).

showLocked.title: Enable Show When Locked
showLocked.body: Toggle Show When Locked ON. This is the key step. Without it, the data stays behind your passcode and is useless to a first responder.

shareCall.title: Enable Share During Emergency Call
shareCall.body: Optional but recommended: toggle Share During Emergency Call ON. When you call 911 (or your local equivalent), your Medical ID is shared automatically with dispatch.

verify.p1: To verify: lock your phone, then on the lock screen press and hold the side button + a volume button. You should see an
verify.p3: at the bottom-left. Your info should appear without unlocking.

android.heading: Android: Emergency information
android.intro: Wording varies slightly by manufacturer (Samsung, Pixel, Xiaomi…), but the location is consistent.

open.title: Open Settings → Safety & emergency
open.body: On older Android versions: Settings → About phone → Emergency information. On Samsung: Settings → Safety and emergency → Medical info.

medical.title: Add medical information
medical.body: Tap Medical info. Fill in blood type, allergies, medications, organ donor, address, medical notes. Same essentials as iPhone.

contacts.title: Add emergency contacts
contacts.body: Back to Safety & emergency → Emergency contacts. Pick people from your address book; the relationship is shown to first responders.

lockScreen.title: Enable lock-screen access
lockScreen.body: Most Android phones expose emergency info via the lock screen Emergency button by default, no toggle needed. On Samsung, double-check Settings → Lock screen → Contact information / Medical info is enabled.

sos.title: Enable Emergency SOS (optional)
sos.body: Settings → Safety & emergency → Emergency SOS. Lets you trigger a call to local emergency services and share location with your contacts by pressing the power button 5 times.

verify.p1: To verify: lock your phone, then on the PIN/pattern screen tap
verify.p3: ) at the bottom. You should see View emergency info or Medical info without entering your PIN.

covers.heading: What Keeplas covers, then
covers.body: Native Medical ID solves the acute case. Keeplas solves the slower one: what happens to your documents, accounts, messages and assets when you become unreachable for days, weeks, or permanently. Two different problems, two different tools, both worth setting up.

recovery.title: Recovery & Inheritance
recovery.intro: Two scenarios, two paths. You lose access while alive: your 24-word phrase or your trust contacts get you back in. You become permanently unreachable: your trust contacts unlock the vault for your recipients.

alive.title: You are alive
alive.pathA: Path A: 24-word phrase → derives your Root Key locally → unwraps your master key. Self-service, no contacts involved.
alive.pathB: Path B: Phrase lost too? Your trust contacts can collaborate to reconstruct the master key (Shamir social recovery).

unreachable.title: You are unreachable
unreachable.body: Life Check fails on every channel → contacts confirm unreachability → 72h grace window → contacts submit their shards → vault opens in memorial mode → recipients receive their content.

words.heading: The 24 words: what they really are
words.p1: At onboarding, your device generates a fresh BIP-39 24-word phrase. Those words are never sent to Keeplas, not even hashed. They exist in three places only: your head, your printed Recovery Kit, and (briefly) your browser memory during onboarding.
words.p2: The phrase feeds Argon2id (a memory-hard key derivation) along with a per-user salt, producing your Root Key. The Root Key wraps your Master Key, which is what actually decrypts your vault. The wrapped Master Key (encryptedKeyBundle) is the only part Keeplas stores, and without your phrase, it's an opaque blob.
words.callout: If you lose your 24 words, your trust contacts cannot recover them, and Keeplas cannot recover them either. What contacts can do is rebuild your Master Key directly via Shamir quorum. After that, you generate fresh 24 words and the vault continues unchanged with a new phrase.

threshold.heading: The recovery threshold
threshold.intro: During onboarding, you split your Master Key into 4 Shamir shares: one device shard and up to three trusted-contact shards. You choose the threshold: the minimum number that must collaborate to reconstruct it. With 2 trusted contacts, keep the threshold at 2; a threshold of 3 needs 3 ready contacts.

three.label: Strict
three.body: Requires three ready contacts. Stronger against a colluding pair, but less forgiving.

threshold.note: Default is 2 trusted contacts, the easiest recovery path while still requiring at least two distinct people. If your contacts face a higher collusion risk (e.g. all from the same family or workplace), use threshold 3 only after 3 contacts are ready.

detection.title: Life Check exhausts every channel
detection.body: Passive signals fail (no app activity, no device unlock, no third-party signal of life). The active channels you configured fire one by one (push, email, WhatsApp, SMS, IVR) with the delays you set. The cycle status moves to escalating.

confirmation.title: Trust contacts mark you unreachable
confirmation.body: All your trust contacts receive a notification asking whether they can reach you. From their hub they see a Mark as unreachable button (only visible while the cycle is escalating). The threshold number of confirmations opens the 72h grace window.

grace.title: 72 hours to come back
grace.body: If you reappear during these 72 hours and click I am well, the cycle is cancelled, the access request is closed and every contact is notified. Nothing ever leaves your vault.

reconstruction.title: Contacts submit their shards
reconstruction.body: When the grace window expires, contacts submit their stored shards. Reconstruction happens entirely on-device. Keeplas servers see only encrypted shards, never the master key. The vault opens in read-only memorial mode.

distribution.title: Recipients receive their content
distribution.body: Items you pre-assigned to recipients (letters, documents, account credentials, contacts) are released to them according to your routing. Anyone you didn't designate sees nothing.

zk.heading: Why this stays zero-knowledge
zk.intro: Throughout the entire lifecycle (distribution, reception, verification, recovery), Keeplas servers never see a raw shard and never see your master key. They store only ciphertext blobs wrapped to specific public keys, plus public metadata (timestamps, audit logs, threshold values).

distribution.label: Distribution
distribution.body: each shard is wrapped to its target contact's ML-KEM public key before it leaves your device. The server stores only the envelope.

reception.label: Reception
reception.body: the contact's browser unwraps the envelope using its locally held private key and persists the raw shard in IndexedDB. Nothing about the raw bytes is ever sent back.

verification.label: Verification
verification.body: successfully unwrapping the shard automatically stamps lastVerifiedAt on the contact's row. That timestamp is just an attestation; the server can't and doesn't inspect the shard.

submission.label: Recovery submission
submission.body: when contacts submit their shard, each one wraps a copy for every peer's public key (fan-out). The server stores the fan-out envelopes, still ciphertext only.

reconstruction.label: Reconstruction
reconstruction.body: the Shamir interpolation that rebuilds the master key happens entirely in the contact's browser. The master key never touches a server, by construction.

zk.callout: Trade-off worth knowing: with threshold = 2, two colluding contacts can both confirm unreachability AND open the vault. The Life Check escalation + the 72h grace window are the only extra safeguards. If you anticipate that risk (e.g. all your contacts share a household), raise your threshold at onboarding.

shardUse.heading: How a contact uses their shard
shardUse.intro: Trust contacts never have to type, copy, export or back up their shard. The browser handles the bytes invisibly. Here's what a contact actually sees and does:

accept.title: They accept your invitation
accept.body: They sign in to Keeplas, generate their own ML-KEM keypair on-device, and the public half is uploaded so you can wrap shards to it.

distribution.title: They visit /shared-with-me once
distribution.body: Their browser auto-unwraps the encrypted shard you distributed and stores the raw bytes in their IndexedDB. The card shows Hash verified [just now]. No button to click.

recoveryTime.title: They click Submit my shard
recoveryTime.body: Either after the post-mortem grace window expires, or after you trigger a social recovery while alive. Their browser reads the local shard, wraps a copy for each peer, uploads the fan-out envelopes.

reconstruction.title: They click Reconstruct master key
reconstruction.body: Once the threshold has submitted, their browser fetches the envelopes addressed to them, unwraps them with their private key, combines with its own raw shard, and rebuilds the master key locally. From there the vault can be decrypted in memorial read-only mode.

crossDevice.heading: What happens if a contact changes device
crossDevice.intro: A trust contact who switches phones, factory-resets their device, opens an incognito window, or signs in on a new laptop does not lose their shard. The architecture handles this without any manual export, copy-paste or special action.

keypair.label: The contact's ML-KEM keypair is portable.
keypair.body: Their secret key is stored on the server, AES-GCM-encrypted under their own master key. As soon as they unlock their vault on the new device (with their 24-word phrase or via Device Unlock), the secret key is decrypted in their browser, ready to use.

shard.label: The encrypted shard is still on the server.
shard.body: Your client wrapped it to their public key during distribution; the ciphertext lives in your trusted_contacts row. It never depended on a specific device.

restore.label: Auto-restoration runs on the next visit.
restore.body: When the contact opens /shared-with-me on the new device, a brief “Restoring your shards…” banner appears while the browser unwraps the server envelope and persists the raw bytes in the new device's IndexedDB. From there, every recovery action works exactly like before.

failure.title: The only failure mode: a contact loses BOTH their device AND their 24-word phrase.
failure.body: Without the phrase, they can't unlock their master key, so they can't decrypt their ML-KEM secret key, so they can't unwrap their shard. Their slot is effectively permanent dead weight. As the vault owner, you should revoke them, invite a replacement, then click Distribute now to issue fresh shards to all current trust contacts.

insights.title: Nine honest cases for digital continuity.
insights.intro: Three reflections, one pain point, two emergency essentials, and three foundations. Skim the table of contents or read top-to-bottom. Each section stands on its own.

if-you-died-today.title: If you died today, who would access what?

secrets-die-with-you.title: Don't let your secrets die with you

probate-vs-grief.title: Probate moves in months. Families need days.

medical-id.title: Set up your phone's Medical ID today

twenty-four-words.title: Your 24 words are the root key

diedToday.p1: Take ninety seconds. Picture every account, file, and key in your life, and then picture them gone. Your phone passcode. Your password manager master key. The drive with the kids' photos. The crypto seed phrase you wrote down somewhere « safe ». The login to the small business email forwarding addressed to your home. Most adults manage more than a hundred online accounts and almost none of them are mapped, named, or transferable.
diedToday.p2: The point of this question isn't to be morbid. It's to turn a vague worry into a concrete checklist. You can't protect what you haven't named. So before you do anything else, write down the categories that matter for your life:

items.identity: Identity & legal documents (passport, ID, birth certificates)
items.people: People (who needs to be contacted, who'd step in)
items.wishes: Wishes (medical directives, organ donor status, funeral notes)

diedToday.p3: Mapping is the act. Choosing who gets what is the gift. The rest of this guide is how Keeplas (and a few habits outside Keeplas) make that gift durable.

secrets.p1: When someone dies without a digital plan, three patterns repeat. The iCloud account quietly freezes. Apple now offers a Legacy Contact, but only if it's set up before death; otherwise the family faces a court order or a permanent lock. Crypto wallets become tombs the moment a seed phrase is missing: there is no support line, no « forgot password », no recovery. Photos and documents on a phone protected by Face ID and an unknown passcode are functionally lost.
secrets.p2: None of these failures need a sophisticated attacker. They happen because the systems we depend on every day are designed for a single living user, not for transfer. The fix is small: a phrase you can write down, a contact who knows where it is, and a tool that can release it on the right conditions.
secrets.p3: That is the ten-minute version of what Keeplas does. Add the few things you would not want to lose, name a trusted contact or two, and the cliff becomes a slope.

probate.p1: Probate, the legal process that grants someone authority over a deceased person's estate, typically takes six to eighteen months, depending on the jurisdiction and the complexity of the estate. In some countries it's faster, in many it's slower. None of those timelines match the speed of life.
probate.p2: Within the first thirty days after a death, the family usually has to: pay the mortgage, keep insurance policies current, contest or confirm subscriptions, file a death notice with banks, and find a dozen account passwords that nobody wrote down. Without prepared access, all of this either falls on one exhausted relative or waits, accruing late fees, lapsing coverage, locking accounts.
probate.p3: Documenting your essentials now isn't a substitute for a will. It's the bridge that gets your family through the first month while the legal machinery catches up. Keeplas releases the information you've curated (not your whole life, just what you chose) to the people you chose, on the timeline you chose.

medicalId.p1: For accidents and sudden illness, the fastest tool is already on your phone: the built-in Medical ID. It lives on your lock screen, works offline, requires no app, and is what trained paramedics actually look for first. Two minutes to set up on iPhone or Android.
medicalId.callout: We deliberately don't replicate Medical ID inside Keeplas: a QR card readable without a key would break our zero-knowledge promise, and the operating system already solved this problem on the device itself.

card.p1: Medical ID is excellent. Paper still beats it in a few specific situations: a dead phone battery, a foreign emergency room where paramedics aren't looking for the iOS lock-screen flow, a phone left in another room, a guardian who needs your blood type read aloud over a phone call.
card.p2: A printed Emergency Card is the offline complement. It carries the bare minimum a first responder or trusted person needs in the first ten minutes, and nothing else. Specifically:

items.identity: Your name, date of birth, blood type
items.contacts: Two emergency contacts with their relationship to you
items.directives: One sentence on advance directives or organ donor status

card.p3: Crucially, none of your vault (no documents, no credentials, no inheritance instructions) appears on this card. The card opens the first door; the rest stays sealed behind your zero-knowledge keys.
card.link: Pick the contacts who go on your card

words.p1: Your 24-word recovery phrase isn't a password. It's the mathematical seed every encryption key on your account is derived from. We use the BIP-39 standard you may have seen in crypto wallets, paired with Argon2id key derivation that turns the phrase into your Root Key locally, on your device. The phrase itself never leaves your device, and Keeplas servers never store it nor any hash of it.
words.p2: That's the strength: the system has no fallback that bypasses the phrase, which is exactly what makes it impossible for us, or anyone we'd be compelled to share with, to read your data. That's also the responsibility: if you lose the phrase and you haven't set up trusted contacts, the vault is gone.
words.p3: The right way to store 24 words is offline, on paper or steel, ideally in two separate physical locations (a fire-resistant box and a sealed envelope at a relative's home, for example). Never store them in a screenshot, a note app, an email draft, or a password manager. Those defeat the entire purpose.
words.link: Generate or print your Recovery Kit

zeroKnowledge.p1: Zero-knowledge is the cryptographic guarantee that a service can store your data without ever being able to read it. In Keeplas, your master key is derived locally from your 24-word phrase and never leaves your device. Every vault item is encrypted with AES-256-GCM on your device before upload. What we hold on our servers is mathematically opaque ciphertext.
zeroKnowledge.p2: The practical comparison: with traditional cloud storage (or most consumer password managers), the service holds a key that can unlock your data. Under a court order, a leaked credential, or a rogue employee, that data becomes legible. With zero-knowledge, the ciphertext stays ciphertext until your device unlocks it.
zeroKnowledge.p3: The implication you should understand clearly: there is no « reset password and recover » path. The two real recovery paths are the 24-word phrase (self-service) and Shamir social recovery via your trusted contacts (when the phrase is lost). That's the whole shape of the system.

trustedContacts.p1: Trusted contacts are the people who can collectively unlock your continuity if you lose your phrase or become unreachable. They don't hold your phrase. They hold cryptographic shards of your master key, generated through Shamir secret sharing. A configurable threshold (2 trusted contacts by default) must agree before recovery proceeds, and reconstruction always happens on their devices, never on Keeplas servers.
trustedContacts.p2: Pick at least two. A third contact adds resilience if you choose the stricter threshold. Pick people in different households, ideally different cities, who would actually pick up the phone in a hard week.

quantumSafe.p1: The biggest cryptographic risk to legacy data isn't today's attackers. It's tomorrow's. The pattern is called harvest now, decrypt later: well-funded adversaries are recording encrypted traffic and stored ciphertext today, betting that a future quantum computer will break the underlying algorithms and let them read what was captured years earlier.
quantumSafe.p2: For consumer chat or short-lived sessions this is mostly theoretical. For inheritance and continuity data, which has to remain confidential for decades, it's a real planning horizon. That's why Keeplas wraps every per-recipient data encryption key, and every Shamir shard, with ML-KEM-768 (NIST FIPS 203), the post-quantum key encapsulation standard ratified in 2024. It replaces RSA-OAEP on the wrapping layer.
quantumSafe.p3: The user-visible impact is essentially zero: same flows, same performance. The future-visible impact is that ciphertext captured today should still be unreadable when post-quantum decryption becomes feasible.

lifeCheckConfirm.invalidTitle: This link is invalid or expired
lifeCheckConfirm.invalidBody: This confirmation link is invalid or has expired. Open Keeplas to confirm from the Life Check page, or wait for the next check-in.

openOnPhone.title: Open this on your phone
openOnPhone.body: Keeplas works on mobile. Open this link on your phone, or scan the QR code shown on this page.

expired.title: This invitation has expired
expired.body: Ask {name} to send you a new link.

security.title: How Keeplas protects your vault
security.intro: Five pillars: how you sign in, how your data is encrypted, how you unlock day-to-day, what happens if you lose access, and the tamper-evident audit trail that makes Keeplas usable as evidence in succession proceedings. We see encrypted bytes, never your data. Every per-recipient key is wrapped with a NIST post-quantum KEM, so a future quantum computer cannot retroactively break what we hold today.

auth.title: Authentication
auth.intro: Email and password sign you in, nothing more. Optional two-factor authentication blocks phishing. Your password never participates in encryption, so resetting it doesn't risk your data.
bullets: Email + password to sign in.
Optional TOTP (Google Authenticator, 1Password, Authy…) for 2FA.
Lost your password? Reset it with your 24 recovery words. Your vault stays untouched.
Lost your authenticator? Reset 2FA with your 24 recovery words.

zk.title: Zero-Knowledge Encryption
zk.intro: Your vault is encrypted on your device, before anything reaches our servers. The keys are derived from 24 recovery words that you alone hold. We never see them, store them, or transmit them. Per-recipient sharing uses a NIST post-quantum KEM, so even a future quantum adversary cannot retroactively decrypt what we hold.
bullets: 24 BIP-39 words generated locally during onboarding.
Argon2id derives a RootKey from your words + a per-user public salt.
RootKey wraps a per-vault MasterKey (AES-256-GCM).
Per-recipient key wrapping uses ML-KEM-768 (NIST FIPS 203), quantum-resistant against future quantum computers.
We see only encrypted envelopes and the public salt. Even if our database leaked, your data stays opaque.

device.title: Device Unlock
device.intro: Typing 24 words at every login is brutal. After your first login on a device, you can save a faster local unlock. It stays on this device only and never syncs.
bullets: Browser: PIN (6+ digits) protected by Argon2id with brute-force lockout.
Phone: Face ID or fingerprint, through the device's secure keychain.
Lose the device? Re-enter your 24 words on a new one.
Inactivity auto-lock: after one hour with no activity the vault locks itself, wiping the in-memory and on-device keys until you unlock again.

recovery.title: Recovery
recovery.intro: Your 24 words are the only way to rebuild your master key. There is no server-side reset, and your trusted contacts never hold any part of it. We have no master key. No backdoor.
bullets: Lost password → reset with your 24 words. Vault unaffected.
Lost 2FA → reset with your 24 words.
Lost the 24 words → trusted contacts hold encrypted shards. A quorum can reconstruct.
Trusted-contact shards are wrapped with ML-KEM-768, so even harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks fail decades from now.
Posthumous continuity → trusted contacts gain access via configurable life-check failures.

audit.title: Legal-Grade Audit Trail
audit.intro: For a court to admit Keeplas as evidence in a succession case, it has to prove who acted, when, and from where, without us being able to forge or rewrite it. Every state-changing action is appended to an immutable, hash-chained log with a server-attested IP and country, and the chain is broken the instant anyone tampers with a single entry.
bullets: Every mutation produces an audit entry with action, resource, timestamp, IP, and country.
IP and country are signed server-side with HMAC-SHA256, so clients cannot spoof their own location.
Each entry carries the previous entry's hash, so the chain can be replayed and verified offline.
At signup we collect your date of birth (legal capacity) and country of residence (applicable inheritance law). Both are stored on your user record and recorded in the audit chain.
We preserve audit logs even after account deletion: the immutable trail outlives the user, which is exactly the property a probate court needs.

cta.prompt: Ready to set up your vault?

faq.a: Attackers would see encrypted bundles, public salts, and server-side scrypt password hashes. None of these alone reveal your vault. Without your 24 words (held only by you) or a quorum of your trusted contacts' shards, the data stays unreadable.

Your vault on-device contains your decrypted MasterKey while you're logged in, so you can export everything. We will publish the encryption format so any developer can decrypt your bundle from your 24 words alone, with no Keeplas involvement.

faq.q: What if I die or become incapacitated?
faq.a: That's the core mission. You configure trusted contacts and a life-check protocol. After confirmed inactivity, your trusted contacts can recover the vault using their distributed shards. You decide who, what, and when.

faq.q: Can a court force you to hand over my data?
faq.a: We can hand over what we have: encrypted bundles. We cannot decrypt them. We do not hold your password reset path, your 24 words, or your MasterKey. The architecture removes the option of complying.

faq.q: Why do I need a password if my data is encrypted by 24 words?
faq.a: Two layers. The password authenticates you to our servers (so attackers cannot just guess emails to access encrypted bundles). The 24 words encrypt the data itself. Both are needed at first login on a new device. Afterward, your device unlock takes over.

faq.q: What encryption algorithms do you use?
faq.a: Argon2id (OWASP 2024 params) for key derivation, AES-256-GCM for symmetric encryption, ML-KEM-768 (NIST FIPS 203, the post-quantum KEM standardized in August 2024) for wrapping per-recipient keys, SHA-256 for verifiers, and Shamir Secret Sharing over GF(256) for trusted-contact recovery. Cryptography runs client-side via the Web Crypto API and @noble/post-quantum.

Yes, end-to-end. Symmetric primitives (AES-256-GCM, Argon2id, SHA-256, Shamir Secret Sharing) are all quantum-resistant by construction. The asymmetric layer, used to wrap per-recipient keys and trusted-contact shards, uses ML-KEM-768, the NIST-standardized post-quantum KEM (FIPS 203, August 2024). This blocks the harvest-now-decrypt-later threat: data we store today stays opaque even to a future adversary running Shor's algorithm on a large quantum computer. Most password managers (Bitwarden, 1Password) have not yet migrated; we built Keeplas post-quantum from day one because vault data must stay confidential for decades.

faq.q: Why do you ask for my date of birth and country?
faq.a: Two legal reasons. Date of birth proves civil capacity (you must be at least 18 to commit your estate) and identifies you in succession proceedings. Country of residence determines which inheritance law applies: French, Belgian, Quebec, and U.S. probate rules differ substantially. Both fields are stored only on your user record and inside the tamper-evident audit chain; they are never used for marketing and never shared with third parties.

faq.q: I was invited as a trusted contact. Why are my email and phone already filled in?
faq.a: Because the person who invited you entered them. To add you, they provide your name, email, and optionally your phone number so Keeplas can send you the one-time invitation link and, later, Life Check alerts. When you accept and create your own vault, those identifiers are pre-filled and locked on the signup form so your account matches the identity they registered, which prevents a mismatched email or number. That is the only information shared about you; nothing from their vault is exposed, and you alone hold your 24 words and keys.

faq.q: Will the audit log hold up in court?
faq.a: That is exactly what it is built for. Every state-changing action is appended to an immutable hash-chained log with a server-attested IP and country (signed via HMAC-SHA256 so a client cannot fake its own location). Auditors and judges can replay the chain offline and detect any tampering: changing a single entry breaks every subsequent hash. Combined with your declared identity (date of birth, country), this is what lets a notary or probate court accept Keeplas activity as evidence of intent and authenticity. The full framework around legally-recognized electronic records in the EU is eIDAS.

Audit entries store action metadata only, never the plaintext of your vault. You can request export or deletion of your account at any time, but the audit chain itself is preserved (anonymized to your now-deleted user ID) so that the immutability guarantee on which a future probate court might rely is not retroactively destroyed. See GDPR full text for the legal basis (Article 6.1.f legitimate interest combined with Article 17.3.b legal obligation).

upcomingFeatures.heading: Upcoming Features
upcomingFeatures.description: No promised dates, only directions we are actively investing in.

items.title: Telegram notifications
items.description: Receive life check-ins and trusted-contact alerts directly in Telegram, with end-to-end encrypted bot delivery.

items.title: SMS notifications & life check-in
items.description: Confirm you're alive with a single SMS reply, and let trusted contacts reach you when network access is limited.

items.title: Data residency
items.description: Choose the country where your encrypted vault is stored, to meet personal, family, or regulatory requirements.

items.title: Vault export
items.description: Download your entire encrypted vault at any time: full portability, no lock-in, no questions asked.

items.title: Notarial & legal compliance
items.description: Optional notarisation of succession instructions and integrations with inheritance frameworks across jurisdictions.

items.title: Blockchain anchoring
items.description: Public proof of existence and tamper-evident timestamps for your most important documents, anchored on a public chain.

items.title: Mobile apps
items.description: Native iOS and Android apps for fast life check-ins, vault access on the go, and biometric unlock.

items.title: Bank-grade audit
items.description: Independent SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certification of our infrastructure, processes, and controls.

items.title: Hardware key support
items.description: Use a YubiKey or any FIDO2 hardware security key as an additional, phishing-resistant authentication factor.

items.title: Personalization
items.description: Tailor parts of the Keeplas experience (themes, notification cadence, vault layout, life-check rhythm) so the app fits how you actually live.

items.title: Estate management
items.description: Tools to plan and orchestrate the transfer of your digital and physical succession to your heirs, with clear roles and step-by-step transmission.

items.title: Succession of estate frameworks, inheritances & holdings
items.description: Manage the transfer of formal structures (holding entities, inheritance dispositions, and corporate shareholdings) with defined beneficiaries and traceable execution.

items.title: Document certification
items.description: Certify the authenticity and integrity of your most important documents, with verifiable proof you can share with third parties.

getApp.heroBody: A private place for your important documents, accounts, instructions and more.

devices.title: Devices and security
devices.subtitle: Manage connected devices and security settings.

deleteAccount.title: Delete your Keeplas account
deleteAccount.heroBody: Delete your account from the app in a few taps. No longer have the app? Send us a request on this page.

inApp.title: From the Keeplas app
inApp.step1: Open Keeplas on your phone and go to Settings.
inApp.step2: Tap Delete my account, then type DELETE to confirm.
inApp.step3: Your account is erased for good 7 days later. Until then, you can cancel from the same screen.

erased.title: What is deleted
erased.body: Everything in your account: your vault (items, notes, files and their history), your contacts and what you share with them, your devices, passkeys and sign-in data, your Life check and your succession plan.
erased.kept: Two records stay after deletion: payment records, for accounting, and the tamper-evident log of security events on the account, for legal and fraud-prevention purposes. Keeplas never could read what was in your vault.

noApp.title: No longer have the app?
noApp.body: Send us a request with the phone number of your account and a way to reach you. We confirm it with you, then schedule the deletion: you are notified and have 7 days to cancel it from the app.
